claims.text: RFC 9110 defines PUT as replacing the target resource's state with the state given in the request; a successful PUT that creates a resource MUST answer 201, and one that replaces an existing resource MUST answer 200 or 204. PUT is listed among the idempotent methods.

RFC 5789 ("PATCH Method for HTTP") defines PATCH as applying "a set of changes" to a resource, contrasted explicitly with PUT's full replacement; the same RFC states PATCH is "neither safe nor idempotent" by default, though one specific PATCH request can be constructed to be idempotent.

RFC 9110 says a successful DELETE should answer 204 when enacted with no further info to supply (200/202 also listed, depending on the case). DELETE is listed among the idempotent methods; a repeated idempotent request's response may differ even though its effect does not.

The Đơn Hàng API at stage-1 has no [HttpPut] or [HttpDelete] endpoint anywhere in the codebase; PATCH /api/v1/orders/{id}/cancel (OrdersController.Cancel) is the only real write endpoint that isn't POST.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at tag stage-1: grep for HttpPut/HttpDelete across all .cs files returns no matches

claims.text: OrdersController.Cancel(int id) has [Authorize] and [HttpPatch("{id:int}/cancel")], takes no request body parameter (only the route id), and its one statement calls orderService.CancelOrderAsync(id) then returns Ok(ToDto(order)).

OrderService.CancelOrderAsync sets the order's Status to "cancelled" and saves, changing no other field of the order (CustomerId, PlacedAt, Items untouched); it also sends a notification on every call, a side effect outside the order's own state.

Live run: after login and creating an order, PATCH /api/v1/orders/{id}/cancel returns 200 with status changed "new" to "cancelled"; the exact same PATCH sent again also returns 200 with an identical body, so this endpoint's change happens to be idempotent in practice.
claims.source_hint: live run this session: curl -i -X PATCH http://localhost:8080/api/v1/orders/<id>/cancel, called twice with the same token

claims.text: RFC 9110 says a client SHOULD NOT generate content in a DELETE request unless the origin server has previously indicated support for it — DELETE normally has no body, but this is a recommendation with an exception, not an absolute prohibition.
The {id:int} route constraint matches only a whole number within the 32-bit range; a non-integer or out-of-range segment matches no route at all.

RFC 9110 9.3.4 requires 201 when a PUT creates the resource and sets no condition on who chooses the id; the lesson's 'only where the client itself picks the id' follows from the client naming the request target, not from a rule in the RFC.
